lessons.title: उजवा (ujvā) — right
lessons.gloss: right (the side) — and the ancient idea that the right hand is the straight one

segments.text: A direction needs a side, and in front of is only one of them.

segments.instruction: say lāmb, then samor, and put a room in front of a house
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say *lāmb*, then *samor*, and put a room in front of a house]

segments.text: उजवा डोळा — ujvā ḍoḷā — the right eye.

उजवा (ujvā) is an adjective, so it comes BEFORE its noun and it agrees with it: उजवा (ujvā) with a masculine noun, उजवी with a feminine, उजवं with a neuter. You have seen that three-way ending before, on माझा / माझी / माझं, and it is the same three endings doing the same job.

Its history is a good one to keep. The Sanskrit word ṛju meant "straight, upright," and the right hand was the straight one — the hand that does the proper thing. The very same idea sits inside Latin rectus and therefore inside English right, which is both a side and a correctness. Two languages made the same joke independently, out of the same root.
To send somebody rightwards you add the -कडे you will meet later, giving उजवीकडे. For now, the side itself is enough.

segments.instruction: ujvī khoolī — and hear the ending follow the noun
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ujvī khoolī* — and hear the ending follow the noun]

segments.prompt: Say 'the right eye', then put the adjective on a feminine noun.

feedback.incorrect: Masculine -ā, feminine -ī: the same three endings as mājhā.

segments.text: Where does उजवा (ujvā) stand relative to its noun? (Before it.) What did its Sanskrit ancestor mean? (Straight — the same idea as English right.)

lessons.title: डावा (ḍāvā) — left
lessons.gloss: left (the side) — the other half of the pair, agreeing exactly as its partner does

segments.text: One side is not a pair. Say उजवा (ujvā) once and then take the other hand.
डावा कान — ḍāvā kān — the left ear.

Everything you learned one lesson ago transfers whole: डावा (ḍāvā) is an adjective, it stands before its noun, and it agrees — डावा (ḍāvā), डावी, डावं. Learning a pair of opposites together is cheaper than learning two words, because the second one costs only its sound.

It opens with ड, the retroflex d, so the tongue curls back the way it does in डोळा. Keep it apart from the dental द of दूध: the two sound close to an English ear and Marathi treats them as different letters entirely.
Now you can take somebody through a door: उजवा (ujvā) or डावा (ḍāvā), then a landmark with समोर or जवळ, and the direction is complete.

segments.instruction: ḍāvā — left, with the tongue curled on the ड
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ḍāvā* — left, with the tongue curled on the **ड**]

segments.instruction: ḍāvī khoolī — and hear the feminine ending
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ḍāvī khoolī* — and hear the feminine ending]

segments.prompt: Say the left ear and the right ear, then swap the noun for a feminine one.
acceptedResponses: ḍāvā kān; ujvā kān; ḍāvī khoolī
डावा कान उजवा कान डावी खोली

feedback.correct: A pair, and one ending rule between them.
feedback.incorrect: Both are adjectives: same three endings, before the noun.

segments.text: Which letter does डावा (ḍāvā) start with, and which taught word shares it? (ड, as in डोळा.) How much of उजवा (ujvā)'s grammar did डावा (ḍāvā) need you to learn again? (None of it.)

segments.prompt: Bend ghar once and run all five postpositions off the same stem.

feedback.incorrect: Say gharā- once, then change only what follows it.

segments.text: What do five of this tranche's words demand of the noun in front of them, and which two do not? (The oblique stem; लांब, उजवा (ujvā) and डावा (ḍāvā) are not postpositions.) Then stop.
